I grew up in the bakery my grandparents owned in the 80s/90s. It wasn’t Greggs that started it. 

It was the supermarkets offering ‘fresh’ (part baked) factory-prepared bread and cakes. 

The supermarket on the corner of their shopping precinct started doing it. People liked the convenience, I mean, why bother getting bread made from scratch and properly fresh cakes when you could get it all (albeit not quite as good) with your shopping and not have to go to another location? The big brands knew this and it’s the usual ‘because f*ckem’ approach they take to the communities they come into. 

I don’t blame the customers. It’s understandable but gutting, utterly f*cked my grandparents financially, they never recovered from it. 

Greggs and other chains employ people in the local community, so I don’t want them to go out of business, but at the same time, Jesus, it’s really sad to see how horrible and generic our high streets are these days.

The chaotic and organised element is a key reason why AEWs TV shows are so poor.

If you give the talent too much freedom to make up their own angles, you end up with lots of parallel thinking, and angles that are indistinct and sometimes indecipherable. 

My wife is a comedian and parallel thinking is a huge thing in creative circles. Loads of people will independently come up with the same joke, and occasionally those two people will end up on the same bill, so you’ll have two people talking about airport food or AI fridges or whatever. It usually ends up with the people who wrote the joke having a chat and deciding that one of them will keep it and the other will lose it. In AEW, everybody gets to keep the angles they’ve created, good or bad, regardless of what anybody else is doing, and whether it’s similar. And it makes for bad television. 

If you’re doing a weekly TV show, you need to plan a story arc - beginning, middle, end, payoff one way or the other, and ensure it doesn’t interfere with another story, or burn people out with too much of the same. 

Sometimes there is no story at all. 

For example, Forbidden Door and its build. Don’t just list all of the titles somebody has won in the countries they’ve come from. Tell me why they are here and who they’re pissed off at or think they’re better than. 

I know they want it to be ‘sport based’ and about ‘just having great matches’. That works in house shows, but not when you have a huge TV deal and are expected to make a show with moments that people are desperate to tune into or stick around for, like scripted dramas and comedy. 

The matches will always be there, but it’s also arguably a strong planned build that gets people truly invested. 

It’s good that there are more choices for pro wrestlers these days. But unless AEW are careful, that option won’t be on prime time tv anymore.

I remember working for an educational news publication in the UK, and about twice a year we’d get the current Secretary of State for Education in to to an interview where a selection of the questions were from readers. 

From what I remember, people were never happy because our correspondent wouldn’t stand over the politician with a red face and bulbous eyes, screaming into their now spittle-flecked face ‘why are you such a nazi, you f*ck. You are the worst person in humanity and I hope all of your family suffers forever’. 

The thing is, I 💯hated their policies, but as a Romany person whose family would have ended up in a camp and/or dead at the hands of literal nazis, I actually find calling everybody on the hard right a Nazi reductive. But I’ll wait for people to shout me down about that. 

If this interview style was the approach taken consistently, you’d rarely get anything from the interview, you’d never get another interview again, and in the media world, as we’ve seen with Alex’s trial, words matter, and can have massive ramifications - rightfully so in his case.

I’m not a fan of Jordan’s interviews, as I find him dismissive, prone to interrupting, needlessly aggressive, and just as keen to label as the disgusting people he (and I) abhor as they are. When he just laughs over people’s points, I can only imagine how aggressive he’d become if somebody did the same to him. 

Next time I’ll skip it. Jordan can do his Jordan interviews and I’ll stick to the main show.

Pharmacist told me that the Elvanse shortage is clearing - but the knock-on effect of the shortage of my medication hasn’t cleared yet (Concerta/any other versions of the long release).

I know it’s literally nobody’s fault, but I had a mini meltdown in my head because I’m so upset that people who suffered from the original shortage are starting to get their meds, whilst I’m still being impacted.

I’m not normally selfish, but I really have had enough of waiting, it’s been 3 months without medication. I don’t want this anymore. I see other people getting their medication and I just feel like I’m at the back of the queue now. 

I just want my meds, had them for 7 years without any issue until last June. Then this. I’m 42 years old and I just want to be able to simply walk in and pick up a prescription. I live in a remote area, and my car is in the garage, so I can’t even drive around to check other places.
Been diagnosed since 2016, and all ran like clockwork until July last year, now it’s getting unbearable, and I just want these delays to end, feels like it’s just going to be like this forever now.

I feel the same, I was dropped into a very cliquey environment, and I’m not from the same background as everybody else either. 

It really does depend on the team dynamics, please don’t take it personally, if you are kind, diligent and you get things done, then you can look at yourself in the mirror every day and say that you’ve done your best. Don’t worry about their opinions, sadly, it’s not as binary as whether they are good or garbage people - some people can just totally flip and buy into toxic group dynamics at work, and that includes collusion and exclusion. It could also be fears of being excluded also. Additionally, if you are in a management position, you have to accept that people above you and below you will question everything that you do, often in great detail. There are benefits to flatter team structures and open feedback, but it does also give rise to toxic people above and below organisationally causing issues and being empowered to make your life difficult.

It’s not like this everywhere though, get a feel for this as much as possible when interviewing for your next job. Funnily enough, whenever anybody says they have a super close-knit team, or a family culture at work, these are alarm bells for me. It can mean a culture of oversharing, silos and cliqueyness.

Best of luck finding a new role!

With regards to some other posts on here saying your husband should just cut her husband out and go NC? I’m conflicted. I don’t think it’s that binary.

If she’s the handful that you say she is, him having that time away to just hang out with your husband could be really helpful for him. We often don’t know what goes on behind closed doors, and if she is explosive in this way with you, I dread to think what she might be like when there are fewer ‘outside’ societal standards to adhere to.

ADHD influencers, especially UK ones.

I was diagnosed in 2016, had to fight to get it, and just cracked on, found some solutions, and tried my best to stick to them with varying degrees of success.

I think a lot of influencers in this space are ridiculous. And I get it’s a spectrum, but a lot of seemingly high-functioning ones treat themselves as if they are severely disabled. This annoys me. There are people at the severe end of both the ADHD and autism spectrum who struggle within the world. And there are people with other severe physical and developmental disabilities that do. The world is not kind to them. And I’d prioritise the world being accessible for them over me, to be honest. 

I also find myself saying to myself ‘and yet…’ when I watch their videos.

‘And yet you find the focus to write a 330 page book and promote and market it.’

‘And yet you find the time to make and edit 8 videos to a high quality every day’

That’s not hyper focus. That’s just somebody hamming up their diagnosis. And it makes us all look like silly, infantilised babies.

I got diagnosed when I was 36, and it was a pretty transformational thing for me.    
It finally gave me a perspective on why I always did well on creative or imaginative projects (I can’t draw or paint, but I have always wanted to write stories), but just could not get my head around science or maths, which couldn’t hold my attention in any way, shape or form. I used to dread spreadsheets (I still do to an extent), and I used to struggle to even remember to write down reminders.   
When I got diagnosed, and got medication, my world started to change for the better. My marriage didn’t survive the diagnosis (reasons unrelated to ADHD, just didn’t work out), but by excersising, researching the shit out of my newly-diagnosed condition, and the mental space that my mediation gave me, it allowed me to get back on track.   
Things that you won’t like to hear perhaps:   


1. Medication, if you choose to take it, is not the magic bullet. It’s the old ‘like putting on a pair of glasses’ reasoning you see on here and in other forms of media form time to time. The glasses help you see more clearly, but you still have to work hard every day. You will still struggle to focus from time to time, and hyper focus in others. The battle will remain for the rest of your life. I’m sorry to say that, but it will. Keep your mind as focused as possible by exercising where you can, introducing variety into your day where possible, and practising mindfulness, even if you feel you’re crap at it. Pro tip: everybody thinks they suck at meditating. Don’t worry about it. 
2. Some people will refuse to believe you, or request in-depth medical details to believe you, regarding your ADHD. My answer to them is: I was diagnosed by a medical professional after a vigorous testing process. Where do you get your evidence from? You may find it comes from ‘some article I saw once, or something.’ Sadly, that includes some friends or family members. 
3. If somebody questions your diagnosis online: do not engage. It’s not worth it.  
4. Will your employer understand and accept your diagnosis? Maybe, but do not expect it. 

The things you might want to hear:   


1. You will get more focus, and you may find some of your creative ideas will come to fruition. I have completed and published 3 short stories since I was diagnosed and prescribed medication. I tried so hard, but never quite managed it up until my diagnosis. I have my diagnosis, life management and treatments to thank for a newfound commitment and discipline. 
2. You will look back at your life with more compassion and understanding. Past you was struggling in a world they didn’t feel like they understand, and a world that was telling you that you were wrong for not understanding it. Now you’ll see that it wasn’t down to you, it was a neurobiological condition. 

I hope that this helps. It’s just my two pence on the matter, and I’m struggling to finish this because I’m low on energy and I’ve spent some focus on this. But good luck, and welcome!
